analysis.one_liner: Funds free, openly licensed college textbooks and expands price disclosures for students.
analysis.headline: Four senators introduced the Affordable College Textbook Act in February 2025, and it has sat in the Senate education committee without a hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a grant program paying colleges and states to develop and expand free, openly licensed textbooks that any student can download and any instructor can adapt, replacing textbooks that can cost students over $1,200 a year in books and supplies. It would also require colleges to disclose on course schedules which materials are free open resources, and require publishers to disclose how digital courseware collects student data. Anything produced with grant money must be released to the public for free, permanently.
analysis.who_benefits: College students, who would pay less for course materials; instructors, who gain free, adaptable materials; and colleges, which receive grant funding. The bill's findings cite a $1,290 average annual budget for books and supplies at four-year public colleges and over a billion dollars a year in potential student savings from open educational resources.
analysis.who_benefits_short: College students paying for course materials

how_it_helps.text: Creates competitive grants to colleges, consortia of colleges, and states to create, adapt, and promote open textbooks that are free to use, reuse, and modify, with priority going to projects that produce the greatest student savings in the highest-enrollment courses.

Requires any textbook or material created with grant funds to be released under a perpetual, royalty-free public license and made available free online in a downloadable, editable format, so the public investment keeps paying off.

Requires colleges to list on online course schedules the retail price, ISBN, and any fees for required materials, flag which materials are free open resources, and post publishers' summaries of how digital textbooks collect and use student data, including whether students can opt out.

Directs colleges to help campus bookstores source lower-cost options and present cheaper alternatives to faculty, and requires a Government Accountability Office report on textbook costs and publisher compliance within three years.

analysis.who_pays: Textbook and digital courseware publishers, who would lose sales as free open textbooks displace paid materials, and taxpayers, who fund the grants. Colleges also take on faculty time for developing and reviewing open materials.

drawbacks.text: The grant program is authorized at 'such sums as are necessary' with no dollar cap, leaving its cost to taxpayers open-ended unless appropriators set a limit.

Creating and maintaining high-quality open textbooks takes faculty time and ongoing updates; the bill requires quality-review and update plans, but coverage for specialized or fast-changing courses can lag behind commercial texts.

Replacing commercial textbooks cuts the revenue that publishers argue funds new editions, supplements, and accessibility work, so the market would shift toward models where quality depends on public and institutional investment rather than sales.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students the benefit is direct and large: free or much cheaper course materials, with price and data disclosures making hidden costs visible. The costs are real but bounded: an open-ended authorization for grants, faculty time to build materials, and lost publisher revenue. A well-run open textbook program has already operated federally since fiscal 2018 under annual appropriations, so this bill mainly makes it permanent rather than inventing a new model.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action has been taken on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Dick Durbin introduced the Affordable College Textbook Act on February 26, 2025, joined by Sen. Angus King (independent), Sen. Tina Smith, and Sen. Ron Wyden.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and the committee has taken no further action on it since.
The bill would give statutory, permanent footing to a grant program similar to the Open Textbooks Pilot, which first received federal funding in fiscal year 2018 through annual appropriations.
The bill's own findings cite new textbook prices rising 82 percent between 2002 and 2012 and a potential for more than a billion dollars a year in student savings from open educational resources.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, textbook and digital courseware sellers benefit, since no program displacing their sales has moved forward, and students gain nothing yet either.

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assigned it to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.

for.name: 2 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Tina Smith and Ron Wyden).

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and has taken no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, has not scheduled the bill for consideration; the record shows no committee action since referral.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-held agenda priorities in the committee left it untouched.

industries.note: Free, openly licensed textbooks would directly displace sales of new-edition print books and digital access codes, which the bill's findings tie to textbook prices that rose 82 percent over a decade. The bill also requires publishers to disclose student data practices in digital courseware.

industries.industry: Campus bookstores and course-material distribution platforms
industries.note: The bill would cut bookstore sales of paid materials but locks bookstores into the new system: grant awards give special consideration to projects that partner with campus bookstores to market and distribute open textbooks, and colleges must help affiliated bookstores source lower-cost options and get course-schedule information.

industries.industry: Open educational resource developers and faculty authors
industries.note: Grant funds would pay for creating, adapting, and studying open textbooks, and give priority to projects that expand adoption beyond the founding institution.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to committee with no cosponsors from the majority party and no committee action after months typically die when the Congress ends. With no Republican support, no hearing scheduled, and the bill's two-year-old predecessor in the last Congress also failing to advance, it is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in this Congress unless sponsors add bipartisan support or the committee takes it up.
